o: A single crate with multiple modules
A collection of related packages that share a Cargo.lock and output directory
A virtual environment for Rust dependencies
A configuration file for cross-compilation
data.e: A Cargo workspace allows multiple packages (crates) to share a single Cargo.lock file and target directory, enabling coordinated builds and dependency management.

data.q: Which key in Cargo.toml defines a workspace at the root level?
o: package
workspace
members
dependencies
data.e: The `[workspace]` table in the root Cargo.toml configures the workspace, including its members and shared settings.

data.q: How do you specify which crates are members of a workspace?
o: List them under the `members` array in `[workspace]`
Add a `workspace = true` field in each member's Cargo.toml
Place them in a subdirectory named `workspace`
Run `cargo add-member <path>` for each crate
data.e: The `members` field (or `exclude`) inside `[workspace]` lists glob patterns for member crate paths.

data.q: What is the default behavior of `cargo build` when run from a workspace root?
o: Builds only the root package
Builds all workspace members
Builds only the first member listed
Fails unless a specific package is selected with `-p`
data.e: By default, `cargo build` (and other commands) operate on all members of the workspace unless a specific package is targeted with `-p`.

data.q: Which command runs tests for all crates in a workspace?
o: cargo test --all
cargo test --workspace
cargo test --members
cargo test
data.e: `cargo test --workspace` runs tests for every member. `--all` is deprecated alias; plain `cargo test` also runs all members from root.

data.q: How do workspace members share dependencies?
o: They automatically inherit all dependencies from the root Cargo.toml
They must declare dependencies individually, but Cargo ensures a single version via shared Cargo.lock
They cannot share dependencies; each member has its own Cargo.lock
They use a global dependency cache configured in `[workspace.dependencies]`
data.e: Each member declares its own dependencies; Cargo resolves a unified dependency graph and writes a single Cargo.lock at the workspace root.

data.q: What does the `workspace.dependencies` table (available in Rust 2021+) allow?
o: Defining dependency versions once and referencing them in members with `workspace = true`
Installing system-level libraries for all members
Overriding the crate registry for the workspace
Specifying build scripts that run for every member
data.e: The `[workspace.dependencies]` table lets you centralize version and feature configuration; members then use `dependency = { workspace = true }`.

data.q: Which flag makes `cargo build` build only a specific package within a workspace?
o: --package <name>
--member <name>
--crate <name>
--only <name>
data.e: `cargo build -p <name>` or `--package <name>` selects a single package. `-p` is the short form.

data.q: What happens if a workspace member specifies a different edition than the root?
o: The build fails; all members must share the same edition
Each member can have its own edition; Cargo compiles each crate with its declared edition
The root edition overrides all members
Cargo emits a warning but uses the member's edition
data.e: Edition is per-crate; members can independently declare `edition = "2021"` or `"2018"` in their own Cargo.toml.

data.q: How can you exclude a crate from a workspace without moving its directory?
o: Add its path to the `exclude` array in `[workspace]`
Rename its Cargo.toml to Cargo.toml.ignore
Set `workspace = false` in its Cargo.toml
Run `cargo workspace remove <path>`
data.e: The `exclude` key in `[workspace]` takes glob patterns to omit crates that would otherwise be matched by `members`.

data.q: What is the purpose of a virtual manifest in a workspace?
o: A Cargo.toml with only `[workspace]` and no `[package]` section, serving as the workspace root
A manifest that downloads dependencies without building
A manifest that defines only dev-dependencies
A manifest used for cross-compilation targets
data.e: A virtual manifest contains only workspace configuration (no `package` table) and acts as the workspace root.

data.q: Which command creates a new workspace with a binary and a library crate?
o: cargo new --workspace myws
cargo init --workspace myws
mkdir myws && cd myws && cargo new --bin app && cargo new --lib lib
cargo generate workspace
data.e: There is no single `cargo new --workspace` command. You typically create a root Cargo.toml with `[workspace]` and then add member crates via `cargo new` in subdirectories.

data.q: How does `cargo publish` behave in a workspace by default?
o: Publishes all members to crates.io sequentially
Publishes only the root package
Fails with an error unless `-p` is specified
Publishes only library crates, skipping binaries
data.e: `cargo publish` from a workspace root requires `-p <package>` to publish a specific member; it does not publish all members automatically.

data.q: What is the effect of setting `resolver = "2"` in `[workspace]`?
o: Enables the new feature resolver that avoids unifying features across packages
Switches to the second version of the Cargo.lock format
Forces all dependencies to use semantic versioning 2.0
Disables dependency resolution for dev-dependencies
data.e: Resolver version 2 (default since Rust 1.51) provides per-package feature resolution, preventing unwanted feature unification across workspace members.

data.q: Which file is shared by all workspace members and should be committed to version control?
o: Cargo.toml of each member
Cargo.lock at the workspace root
target/ directory
.cargo/config.toml
data.e: The workspace root Cargo.lock records the exact dependency versions for reproducible builds and must be committed.

data.q: How can you run a specific binary from a workspace member without installing it?
o: cargo run --bin <name> --manifest-path <member>/Cargo.toml
cargo run -p <package> --bin <name>
cargo execute -p <package> --bin <name>
cargo start --package <package> --bin <name>
data.e: `cargo run -p <package> --bin <name>` runs the specified binary from the given package within the workspace.
